final_proof:
To prove that the set of $p$-adic numbers $\mathbb{Q}_p$ is uncountable, it suffices to show that it contains an uncountable subset. We consider the set of $p$-adic integers, denoted by $\mathbb{Z}_p$, which is a standard subset of $\mathbb{Q}_p$.

Every $p$-adic integer $x \in \mathbb{Z}_p$ can be expressed as a formal infinite power series in $p$:
$$ x = \sum_{i=0}^{\infty} a_i p^i $$
where the coefficients $a_i$ are integers chosen from the set $\{0, 1, 2, \dots, p-1\}$. 

This representation is known to be unique for each $p$-adic integer. That is, two $p$-adic integers are equal if and only if their corresponding sequences of coefficients $(a_0, a_1, a_2, \dots)$ are identical. 

Because of this unique representation, we can establish a natural bijection between the set of $p$-adic integers $\mathbb{Z}_p$ and the set of all infinite sequences $(a_0, a_1, a_2, \dots)$ with terms in $\{0, 1, \dots, p-1\}$. This set of sequences is precisely the Cartesian product $\{0, 1, \dots, p-1\}^{\mathbb{N}}$.

Since $p$ is a prime number, we have $p \ge 2$, meaning the set $\{0, 1, \dots, p-1\}$ has at least two elements. By Cantor's diagonal argument, the set of infinite sequences over any finite alphabet of size 2 or greater is uncountable. Therefore, the set of sequences $\{0, 1, \dots, p-1\}^{\mathbb{N}}$ is uncountable.

Since there is a bijection between this uncountable set of sequences and $\mathbb{Z}_p$, it follows that the set of $p$-adic integers $\mathbb{Z}_p$ is uncountable.

Finally, because $\mathbb{Z}_p$ is a subset of $\mathbb{Q}_p$ ($\mathbb{Z}_p \subseteq \mathbb{Q}_p$), and any set containing an uncountable subset must itself be uncountable, we conclude that the set of $p$-adic numbers $\mathbb{Q}_p$ is uncountable.
